[quote=qianxun;61489596][spoiler=[b]Revolution as an institution? | ZJ[/b]]
[list]from: Shangguan Zhenjin <znjasnobres@falaralto.ta>
to: cj111@uq.edu.qi
date: 27 Oct 2028, 08:11
mailed-by: falaralto.ta
signed-by: falaralto.ta
security: high level[/list]

My question then is this, Mr. Cui:

In all communist governments (or which you call "socialist governments", "people's democratic governments", or some other terminology, for you denigrate the designation of "communism" for anything by the final triumph of your cause), there is invariably the use of the term called "revolutionary". A revolution is a great reverberation, if you may agree with my definition. It is to my understanding that all revolutions in history have been called such retroactively, and anything that does not triumph in the moment of disorder is merely a disturbance, some crisis or internal conflict, or else a protest. A revolution is a great changing of the systems of the state inasmuch as historiography may sometimes lament at the time periods before and after its occurrence.

A revolution, therefore, is the moment. When it is over, why still do your governments persist in calling itself the revolution and its supporters the revolutionaries, when the duties that had been ascribed to it at the moment of triumph is now over?

[/spoiler]

[spoiler=[b]Semantics and the Purpose of Revolution[/b]]
[list]from: Cui Jin <cj111@uq.edu.qi>
to: znjasnobres@falaralto.ta
date: 27 Oct 2028, 11:03
mailed-by: falaralto.ta
signed-by: falaralto.ta
security: high level[/list]

Dear Princess Imperial,

Forgive the semantic argument, but this will be important in my response. A revolution is never simply the changing of the guard, but the long, drawn-out, sometimes terrible, sometimes heroic, and always difficult transformation that comes after, when the people's revolution must now lay down its arms and take up the positions of power to reform the whole of society towards the great and vindictive battle against the imperialist systems upon which this very revolution came about. Until then, the revolution exists as an institution of the new society that changes and continues to change until the classless, stateless society emerges.

Therefore, socialist governments only abandon the term "revolutionary" when one of two things occur: A counter-revolution successfully emerges and reinstates the old tyranny, or else we succeed in forming the new man in a communist society.

[/spoiler]

[spoiler=[b]Masses =/= revolution? | ZJ[/b]]
[list]from: Shangguan Zhenjin<znjasnobres@falaralto.ta>
to: cj111@uq.edu.qi
date: 27 Oct 2028, 11:15
mailed-by: falaralto.ta
signed-by: falaralto.ta
security: high level[/list]

So a counter-revolution, massed by the common people, perhaps even proletariat, who succeeds in storming through the palace of a socialist government, who overwhelms its regular armed forces through an awesome feat of arms, cannot itself be considered revolutionary?

[/spoiler]

[spoiler=[b]Yes[/b]]

[list]from: Cui Jin <cj111@uq.edu.qi>
to: znjasnobres@falaralto.ta
date: 27 Oct 2028, 13:38
mailed-by: falaralto.ta
signed-by: falaralto.ta
security: high level[/list]

A counter-revolution, by its very definition, opposes the liberation of the people and the destruction of the old systems. And yet, it is not in my power to proclaim to the counter-revolutions to halt their misuse of the term "revolution", since it is their very purpose to pervert its meaning, nor can I ever guarantee that the proletariat is able to always be a person of complete and total reason, for to presume absolute rationality to all living things is lunacy. In the state of nature we seek our needs, sometimes wretchedly, and once sated we seek our wants, sometimes savagely. Even the proletariat might wage a violent war to restore their own chains if it means successfully retreating into the illusory comforts of the old master. There can be no true revolutionaries except for those that understand the ideals of the communist society.

[/spoiler]

[spoiler=[b]Single-mindedness in the revolution | ZJ[/b]]

[list]from: Shangguan Zhenjin <znjasnobres@falaralto.ta>
to: cj111@uq.edu.qi
date: 27 Oct 2028, 15:47
mailed-by: falaralto.ta
signed-by: falaralto.ta
security: high level[/list]

So it's the socialist definition to simply reject all other viewpoints as evil. Don't you think that this way of thinking is why the world constantly anathemizes you?

If the revolution is an institution, as in a government persisting through an indefinite period of time until the classless society, and if its mission is to create the 'new man,' then by your own logic, any opposition to that institution is not merely political dissent, but a symptom of false consciousness. You are not compelled to see them as citizens exercising a political will, however misguided. You are compelled to see them as a disease to be cured, or an enemy to be crushed, for the sake of their own future freedom. And then will come soft rains and the dead on the ground, shot to death by your own "revolutionary army", in pursuit of the darkest and most single-minded liberation.

During that long transformation, who decides what the people truly need versus what they merely want in their 'savagery'? If it is always the institution itself, the self-proclaimed vanguard of the revolution, then have you not simply replaced the old master with a new one?

[/spoiler]

[spoiler=[b]Discussion and story (last response for now)[/b]]
[list]from: Cui Jin <cj111@uq.edu.qi>
to: znjasnobres@falaralto.ta
date: 1 Nov 2028, 5:56
mailed-by: falaralto.ta
signed-by: falaralto.ta
security: high level[/list]

I will tell you a story, Princess Imperial. It concerns a certain Sanguinian acquiantance I met from way back during my winter stay at Citharo. 

He was a good gentleman, from a wealthy family, who by the excellence of his birth had been destined to inherit a family enterprise that had been in operation since the 16th century. However, man has a tendency to rebel against the path that had been set for him, and this good friend of mine opted to live a life in constant and costly adventure. Princess Imperial, have you ever climbed mountains? I haven't. I think only madmen dare to rose to these hostile hellscapes.

You traverse narrow ridges in the shadow of total darkness, at risk of stumbling and taking out your whole group in the mighty winds, or else straying so far and become entrapped in an airless crevice until you're gone, and many have gone.

Some madmen conquer mountains if to be simply exonerated from the charge of having turned back, and yet here are so many horrible fates that await them. And yet men conquer mountains still, as with this friend of mine, now tired and breathing heavily as he dangles against the jagged rock and stone of Mount Palamina, under which is the eternal abyss, and with great effort he thrusts himself up and he breathes steadily but decides that it was only near to the hour of death that his felt truly alive. Then, it is over. He is fatigued but happy, and while he is content to have triumphed over the challenge that he had set for himself, the dream is over, supplanted in turn by a distant memory. 

I am certain, and will remain certain for the rest of my life, that living in general seems to be predestined towards something approaching misery. Before our time, men savaged the weak and took what was needed to survive. We say now that the primal nature of man has been sated by this thing called civilization, but who determines the civility of societies if not those that have long since triumphed from their conquests? Who have impelled the many to observe this hegemony that is called liberality, which liberates only those with the means and the will to devour the world, now restrained to instead destroy the human race from a distance. 

These "civilized men" take from the labor of the proletariat, they drain the vitality of the workers with the money of their fathers and their father's fathers and reap the great returns for the great merit of their wise investments, while the producers of the goods are let to starve in the cities they've made. 

Therefore, the revolution can only be rationality, and the counter-revolution can only be irrationality.

[/spoiler][/quote]

[spoiler=[b]In Case of Drowning[/b]][b]In Case of Drowning | 1 November 2028[/b]

I sometimes wonder if I'm just sleepwalking through life.

Even now, even here, my feet beneath a beautiful tiled floor and the cool ambience of a humming air conditioner, a nice cup of freshly brewed coffee mixed in with a little bit more milk than what's acceptable to snops, a nice dress, and a wonderful view of the great White Sea, I feel empty. It's a strange feeling, to be given everything you've ever wanted from the moment of your birth, to have the time and resources to pursue virtually ever single dream you've ever imagined under the Sun. I've seen the commons sacrifice so much to have a bare fraction of what I've had, and yet, am I even grateful for anything that's been given to me?

Consider this the inane, insane ramblings of an ivory tower elite, but I sometimes romanticize what it means to live in the commons. To have no reason to speak to anyone when you start your day, and to be impelled with your own agency to begin pursuing a specific set of tasks for the day. Or to not pursue them at all, if you wish. I've never had much agency, not at least as the Princess Imperial.

"If it means a lot to them," I'd always say, as I settle down in the changing room and dress up in those ridiculous ceremonial outfits the other Shangguan princes insist I wear. Who still wears a chenyi in this day and age? And in Elseyr of all places? I know the commons would not envy me at all for being unable to choose my own clothes, I'm certain at least by that much.

I'm very rich. Ludicrously so. According to some estimates I'm the wealthiest Qianxun at the moment. Though, those statistics are sort of misleading, since all those fancy tabloid sites always cite me as the head of the House of Shangguan. Ergo, all assets of the house fall under my name, which obviously isn't the case. Not that the princes try to correct that, of course. Why bother having to publicly report your financial affairs, when you could just put my name instead and leave me with all the liabilities, right?

I live very comfortably. I eat well, I'm fit, I'd like to think I'm decently smart, and people rarely conteset me if I say I want this thing or I want to learn that activity. All good then!

Except I've been quite miserable and empty, as I said in the beginning of this brief rant. The gigantic caveat to this life I'm currently living is that I can be anyone I want to be as long as it never, ever overshadows what the House wants me to be: an emperor. And yes, I do go by the male title, since in the Qianxun language there isn't actually a equivalent female title for the 單于. Fun fact.

But anyways, an emperor, living out in exile because your intended empire is currently communist! So in short, I needed to be the most refined and most elegant unemployed person that ever lived. No close confidants (without House supervision), no public statements (without House supervision), no happiness (without House supervision). Oh, did I mention that I needed House supervision? I did? Alright, I just felt like I needed to clarify. So yeah, all that glitters isn't gold.

That said, I have been finding my own little inklings of freedom lately. For one thing, this entire time I've been ranting to you, dear viewer, I've been largely left alone in this big, beautiful mansion that the Shangguans dumped me in to prevent me from causing trouble. Sure, it gets lonely, but a connected world allows you to do more than just mope around pathetically in the dark corner, like talking to friends. Or, well, in my case, literal enemies,

[b]- - -[/b]

In case of drowning, always consider the extra work you're springing onto the government.

Cui Jin hadn't been sleeping well. He never actually slept well ever, but he also isn't now. He listed over to the side, the faint light of his laptop monitor quietly staring back at him, its internal fans blaring ominously from having been left running and charging for the entirety of the previous night. Before he could completely fall over, however, he is awakened to a light tap on the back of his head.

"Keep doing that and you'll end up breaking something important Mr. Party Secretary," said Zhang Meihui, sighing as she calmly pushed Cui back into an upright position.

"I never took you for the caring type," jested Cui, blinking his eyes back aggressively as he looked over to check the time. "What... what time is it?"

"Don't worry Mr. Party Secretary, I was talking about your laptop," she sardonically replied. "And it's nine in the morning."

"Not great, not terrible, better than yesterday at least."

Better than yesterday, he said. That was probably an understatement in more ways than one. It hasn't been a very wonderful time for Cui Jin since the mess at Qianxun Major, having to listen to the victim impact statements, strongly-worded letter after strongly-worded letter asking for justice, apologies, and compensation. Cui Jin's laptop was even left on an email draft asking for more time to respond to a very basic point of inquiry.

Cui Jin leaned forward into his laptop and typed up a mediocre continuation to the draft, then had it sent without any care for its recipient, then continued on to the next email. Another inquiry, asking how long it'll take for the investigation to start explaining finer points of contention. "Direct this to the party committee", Cui lazily writes, then sending again.

"You're just blazing through them." Zhang says, a concerned twinge in her voice.

"It's not easy losing a loved one." said Cui Jin, almost sounding sincere, "It's not easy trying to calm down people who've lost said loved ones either. All this, while I myself am also trying to get some answers out of Director Kang."

"Has the Director said anything yet?"

"He's been avoiding my calls entirely; it's ridiculous. I'd send a complaint to my uncle, but he probably considers the Director more of his nephew than I am."

"I... don't know what to say?"

"It would've been strange if you did."

After a momentary and awkward silence, Cui raised his arm towards Zhang and beckoned her closer. Nodding, she grabbed hold of an office chair and scooted over near him, peering over his laptop to see the small little red dot that acted as the notification for some fairly important. It was yet another email, but the subject matter was rather unique. Unique, in that it had none of the usual keywords in the recent mess. Nothing about "inquiry", "missing", "help" or anything like that. Instead, it was on the topic of revolution, or to be specific a formula for revolution.

"The Princess Imperial?" Zhang said quizzically, tilting her head with a clear frown. "I'm surprised the MZP haven't caught on to this. Why do you keep talking to her?"

"Consider it morbid curiosity." Cui said, opening the notification and quickly reading over the email's terse contents. "With how much the MZP's been stonewalling my attempts to understand what went down in the lakes, my brain's been very hard at work exoticizing everything that hasn't got anything to do with us, [i]nánmán [/i]included. Besides..."

"Besides...?"

"Apparently, the Princess Imperial and the rest of the Shangguans seem to know something about the lakes."

Hearing that, Zhang blinked once. Twice. She took off her glasses and cleaned her eyes, though she was really trying to understand if her ears had heard right. "The Shangguans?" she asked, clearly incredulous. "What exactly would some out-of-touch exiled royals know about researchers randomly drowning studying the lakes? The last time the Shangguans interacted with the lakes, the whole thing was still just used for fisheries."

"As it turns out," Cui replied, his voice suddenly dropping low. "... quite a lot, actually. A lot more than I was expecting, let alone from some sheltered princess."[/spoiler]
